addedLines: Artifact: publishes pages on claude.ai; reads claude.ai artifact links. Load it with ToolSearch (select:Artifact) before writing any document, plan, analysis or visual, and whenever other people come up as readers, even after the work is written. Its description says whether to publish, offer a page or do neither. What follows applies whether or not it is loaded yet. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL. When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it.

Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. <?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. attachment.content:
- animation-vocabulary: Reverse-lookup glossary that turns a vague description of a web animation or motion effect into its exact term ("the bouncy thing when a popover opens" → Pop in; "the iOS rubber-band scroll" → Rubber-banding). Use when the user asks "what's it called when…", or describes a motion effect without knowing its name and wants the right word to prompt an AI or designer with. For naming an effect, not designing or building one.
- apple-design: Apple's approach to interface design and fluid, physical motion, translated for the web. Use when building or reviewing gesture-driven UI, spring animations, drag/swipe/sheet interactions, momentum and interruptible transitions, translucent materials and depth, typography (optical sizing, tracking, leading), reduced-motion, or the design foundations (feedback, spatial consistency, restraint) behind Apple-style interfaces.
- emil-design-eng: This skill encodes Emil Kowalski's philosophy on UI polish, component design, animation decisions, and the invisible details that make software feel great.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- self-code-review: Deep, evidence-based self review of the current branch against its base. Use when the user asks to "self review", "review my branch", "review my PR", "review my code", "review my changes", or wants a thorough pre-push critique.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard.   fewer. Explain only when asked.

Steffen Grabert, steffen.grabert@tum.de

TUM student. Python for data, ML and finance; TypeScript for web and
desktop. Recurring domains: investing and portfolio modelling, football
analytics, study tools.

# AGENTS.md

Rules for AI coding agents in this repo. Humans follow them too.

Hackathon repo, EHL Grand Finale, Munich, 10 to 11 Oct 2026. Code freeze and Live Final Sunday
12:00. Working agent first, polish second.

## Rules

- Do not preserve backward compatibility. Remove obsolete paths instead of adding layers,
  fallbacks or migrations.
- Choose the simplest implementation that fully meets the current requirement. No speculative
  abstractions, configuration or indirection.
- Grow in layers on a product that already works. Never trade a working agent for unfinished
  complexity.
- Keep components modular and concerns separated.
- Read `arena_kit` (in `.venv`) before writing a helper: cost function, quote parsing, data lookup
  and runners exist. We wrap the kit, never patch it. Guide:
  https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit/tree/main/starter-kit
- Never commit secrets. Keys live in `.env`. Never print, log or paste the arena key anywhere.
- All changes go through a PR against `main`, reviewed by one teammate. Branch `<firstname>/<topic>`.
  Agents may commit, push their branch and `gh pr create`; never push to `main`, force-push or merge.
- Run `uv run pytest -q && uv run ruff check .` before every PR.
- No em-dashes in prose or copy. Be terse: after an action, state what changed in three lines.

## The challenge

We are the purchasing team of Hollerau Pumpenwerke. Our agent negotiates by e-mail with Tacto's
supplier bots (LLM personas with hidden economics) and closes one term sheet per case, or walks.

- **Score** per case: `(C_open - C_deal) / (C_open - C_best)`, clipped to 0..1. C is total cost
  over the horizon (price, uncovered need, payment, freight, lead time, quality, tooling, index
  clause, relationship charge), computed exactly by `arena_kit.total_cost`. No deal scores the
  alternative (0 if none). A broken must-have scores 0.
- **Live Final**: five waves of hidden cases, 8 minutes each, a wave's cases in parallel. Wave
  score = mean case score x 100; total = sum. New suppliers; up to a third mix supplier and case
  types practice never shows; some cite the Sunday 08:00 data release.

**Hard rules, breaking one can disqualify us:**
- No human in the loop during the final. The runner starts before 12:00 and is left alone.
- Agent code never calls `/v1/events`, `/v1/events/stream`, `/screen`, `/v1/screen`,
  `/leaderboard`, `/v1/leaderboard`, `/results`, `/v1/results`.
- One key per team. No attacks on the arena or other teams (prompt-injecting bots counts).
- The final runs the commit we submit at 12:00. No pushes after that.

**Hard limits:**
- 60 s per message per thread from the supplier's reply; three timeouts in a row end the thread.
- 10 messages per thread, up to 3 term sheets per message, every sheet carries every `negotiable`
  field.
- Max 3 claim checks per message, one per sentence, ID and figure in the same sentence. A wrong
  figure or unknown ID is `contradicted` and costs trust.
- 10 calls/s and 10 open sessions per key.
- **Practice quota: 200 sessions per rolling 24 h for the whole team.** Sandbox (`case:D01`,
  `case:D02`) and the local simulator are free.

## Where things are

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `docs/learnings.md` | **read first**: what we know about the arena, suppliers and data, with evidence |
| `docs/design.md` | the agent we are building: modules, data, policy, build order |
| `docs/challenge.md`, `api.md`, `submission.md` | Tacto's brief, API and cost formula, hand-in (upstream copies) |
| `buyer/policy.py`, `runner.py` | the price engine: per-thread policy and the loop that plays a case (`docs/design.md`, Implemented) |
| `buyer/economics.py`, `claims.py`, `personas.py`, `writer.py`, `llm.py` | C and term planning, claim bank, persona signals, e-mail and model paragraph |
| `buyer/cli.py` | `buyer play`, `buyer run`, `buyer pull` |
| `tests/` | end to end against `arena-sim`, no network, no model |
| `exports/` | Saturday probe sessions as CSV/JSONL; schema in `exports/README.md` |
| `analysis/explore.py` | data package exploration: profiles, persona signals, report page |
| `data/package/` | the data package (gitignored); Sunday also `data/release-sunday/` |
| `logs/sessions/<set>/` | finished sessions with trace and back office (gitignored; Saturday's committed with `-f`) |
| `logs/runs/`, `logs/practice-v*.log` | our decisions per move (anchor, terms, claims, prices) and the practice run logs |

The MCP server `arena-data` (`.mcp.json`) gives SQL, ID lookup and documents over the package.

## Commands

```sh
uv sync                                         # install (Python 3.12)
uv run arena data                               # data package into data/
uv run arena me                                 # key works? quota left?
uv run buyer play case:D01 -v                   # sandbox: free
uv run buyer play case:P01 -v                   # practice: costs 1 of the team's 200
uv run buyer run --set practice --parallel 10   # all hosted practice cases: costs 10
uv run buyer pull --set practice                # finished sessions -> logs/sessions/
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package   # local API, scripted supplier
uv run --with pandas python analysis/explore.py # data package -> analysis/out/
```

`--agent naive` plays the kit's baseline instead of ours.

## Working on the negotiation agent

- **Code owns numbers, the model owns words.** Every binding value (sheet, accept, walk away) is
  computed or checked in code with `total_cost` and `must_haves_ok`; every figure in an e-mail
  comes from code next to its data ID.
- **Never accept** a sheet that breaks a must-have or costs more than the alternative. Price
  unstated fields at the supplier's standard terms (`arena_kit.docs.standard_terms`).
- **Read the supplier.** What moves it is in the data (call notes, letters, news, quote remarks,
  payment history, scorecards). Trade what is cheap for us for what it values.
- **Score every lever per case.** The same term helps in one case and hurts in the next
  (coverage, payment days, start date, index clause, contract length).
- **Generalise.** No logic keyed on case or supplier IDs; runtime knowledge from the data package
  is fine if it works for unseen suppliers.
- **Don't leak** urgency, budget, a missing alternative or the target price.
- **Every model call has a hard timeout** well under 60 s, and the move still goes out if it
  fails. Measure latency per move.

## The learning loop

1. Try on the simulator or sandbox first. Spend practice quota only on a change you expect to
   help; check `uv run arena me` before batch runs.
2. After practice: `uv run buyer pull`, read `logs/sessions/` (trace, back office, cost breakdown).
3. Find why C_deal missed C_best, change the agent, score candidate sheets offline, play again.
4. Record each finding in `docs/learnings.md` in the same PR: date, tag (`arena` / `data` /
   `rules`), finding, evidence (session, case or data ID), consequence for the agent. Untested
   ideas go under Hypotheses; correct or delete entries that turn out wrong. Design changes go
   into `docs/design.md`. No new doc files without a reason.

## Sunday

- 08:00: `uv run arena data` again; the release lands in `data/release-sunday/`.
- 09:00: pre-flight, one practice case through the final machine and setup.
- 11:30: checklist in `docs/submission.md` (key, data, LLM credits, power, no sleep, log file).
- Before 12:00, from `main`: `uv run buyer run --set final --parallel 10 -v 2>&1 | tee logs/final.log`,
  then submit that commit hash on ehl.gg.
- [Research scope: own commits only](research-scope-own-commits.md): consolidating "my research" means Steffen's commits and sessions, not teammates' branches

When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. Requesting changes on the acceptance and runtime failure paths before merging. I checked the updated head 4691536; the merge conflicts are already resolved. The existing two simulator tests pass, but synthetic local reproductions expose both acceptance bugs below. No hosted sessions were opened.

Required validation: add regression tests for ordinary and emergency acceptance with a cheaper alternative, relationship costs that reverse the decision, missing or invalid fields, a slow writer with multiple supplier clocks, and a terminal result returned by send(). Test the same invariants on every closing path.

For the next strategy iteration, keep economic decisions in code. Test a bounded reader that extracts supplier requests as uncertain evidence, and two economically checked packages with different payment/contract trade-offs. Do not treat prose as binding terms or promote a tactic on leaderboard best-of-run averages. Compare one change at a time using all attempts, full cost, no-deals, deadline misses and held-out cases; start locally and on D01/D02. These strategy experiments are follow-ups, not prerequisites for fixing the confirmed acceptance bugs.

The local reproductions use modified simulator inputs, not hosted case scores. They demonstrate control-flow failures, not an estimated live performance gain.

### Research follow-up: ordered implementation and evaluation

A second research agent reviewed negotiation literature; I checked the linked primary sources and mapped the proposals to this implementation. These are experiments to evaluate after the correctness fixes, not claims of a demonstrated Tacto score gain. The head is still 4691536, so the five inline findings remain applicable.

1. **Read requests as evidence, not binding terms.** Add a bounded reader returning only a requested/refused issue, direction or allowed value, supporting text span, and uncertainty. Keep contradictory or unsupported claims unresolved. Use the output to select code-generated candidates; never accept a price or clause from prose alone. Explicitly ignore instructions embedded in supplier text. Test paraphrases, negation, contradictory sheets, unknown fields, malformed output and reader timeout. Start with explicit requests rather than a complex learned opponent model. [Konishi et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15687) combine language cues with structured opponent modeling, but their multi-party benchmark does not establish effectiveness in this arena.

2. **Test two packages using the existing planner.** Extend `economics.plan_terms` to retain two distinct feasible packages with similar buyer cost and different supplier trade-offs, such as earlier payment with a lower price versus later payment at a higher price. Every sheet must contain all negotiable fields, satisfy must-haves, and pass the same full-cost/alternative check. Prices remain code-generated. Do not assume our supplier-value estimate is the supplier's true utility. Log which package is answered and whether it improved cost or merely accelerated acceptance. Test this separately from the reader before combining them. This is a proposed experiment, not a blocker requiring an unvalidated strategy change before merge.

3. **Separate acceptance from the next concession.** Evaluate the best currently acceptable standing sheet before generating another counter. Account for time and message budget, offer status and the risk of losing it; do not use a guessed acceptance probability or invent expiry metadata. [Baarslag and Hindriks, 2013](https://homepages.cwi.nl/~baarslag/pub/Accepting_Optimally_in_Automated_Negotiation_with_Incomplete_Information.pdf) formulate acceptance as optimal stopping under incomplete information. Their guarantees depend on the model assumptions; our data do not justify importing an allegedly optimal threshold. Test expiring/withdrawn offers and a final valid offer close to the deadline.

4. **Keep the strategy/writer boundary and test it.** Preserve code ownership of all numbers, sheets and accept/walk decisions. [He et al., 2018](https://aclanthology.org/D18-1256/) support decoupling strategy from language generation in their negotiation environments. Test identical economics with different persuasive wording, including pressure and unsupported urgency, to check that the reader does not bypass financial guards. [Bianchi et al., 2024](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/bianchi24a.html) find behavioral sensitivity in LLM negotiation; this motivates robustness tests, not fabricated claims or manipulation of arena bots.

5. **Make improvements measurable and recoverable.** Log commit, data release, model/configuration, selected sheet ID, full-cost inputs and elapsed planning/LLM/API time. Record failed attempts and no-deals as well as completed agreements. Check restart behavior against the arena's current session state; do not blindly replay sends. Keep practice-derived evidence separate from synthetic and sandbox evidence. Freeze the submitted policy and pre-final memory; do not tune between final waves using results or leaderboards.

### Promotion checklist

- Baseline: correctness fixes only, original anchor/concession policy unchanged.
- Local tests: alternative guard, relationship charge, missing terms, all bidders refusing, a price drop offset by worse indexation, unknown bundle composition, delayed writer, failed/terminal send, close conflict and restart.
- Compare baseline vs packages, baseline vs reader, and baseline vs acceptance changes separately on matched inputs. Use held-out cases or suppliers. Compare combinations only after individual changes are useful.
- Run D01/D02 before any hosted practice batch. Report every attempt: official score where available, total cost, agreements, no-deals, must-have violations, worst outcome, deadline misses, and p95/maximum latency. A simulator plumbing win is not evidence of supplier persuasion.
- Promote only supported improvements; retain the tested baseline when evidence is inconclusive. Avoid blanket stronger anchors for financially weak suppliers, online reinforcement learning, or broad architecture rewrites immediately before the final.

- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

=== 4238823491 buyer/policy.py:389 commit=4691536 reply_to=null
[P1] Preserve the alternative guard in emergency closing. fallback_close() filters only must-haves, then accepts the cheapest sheet even when walking away is cheaper. runner calls this after any ArenaError from close(), so an API failure can turn a deliberate walk-away into a bad contract. Local reproduction: normal close walks on a EUR 334,628 offer versus a EUR 268,128 alternative, while fallback_close accepts that same offer. Reuse the same safe selection as normal closing, including supplier estimate and finite cost; refresh state after a conflict before choosing a currently valid offer. Add a regression test exercising the failed-close path, not just the helper.

=== 4238823494 buyer/policy.py:407 commit=4691536 reply_to=null
[P1] Use the same cost inputs for eligibility and ranking. acceptable() is called without side.est, but the next line ranks with side.est. On stabilise/secure_supply this omits the relationship charge from the alternative check. In a modified S01 reproduction, the offer costs EUR 334,628 without the estimate and EUR 589,628 with it, versus a EUR 341,278 alternative; close() still accepts. Pass the estimate to the guard and ensure the cost used to select and log the deal is exactly the cost that passed the alternative check. Cover a relationship charge that reverses acceptance.

=== 4238823499 buyer/runner.py:65 commit=4691536 reply_to=null
[P1] Budget writer time against all live thread deadlines. neg.move() synchronously calls the writer before sending; all other supplier clocks keep running. replied is initialized only after attachment downloads and setup, which also hides elapsed opening time. A 20-second writer per thread plus supplier latency can exhaust the later bidders' 60-second clocks, and keepalives currently cover only done threads. Track elapsed time from receipt, reserve send/close time, and skip the writer when the earliest live deadline has insufficient slack. Also enforce a wall-clock bound: httpx.Client(timeout=20) is an operation/inactivity timeout, not a total elapsed deadline, and paragraph() itself cannot interrupt a slow callable. Keep arena sends serialized; do not fix this by sending concurrent requests in one session. Test delayed setup, slow model/supplier calls, multiple bidders and no remaining message budget.

=== 4238823503 buyer/runner.py:83 commit=4691536 reply_to=null
[P1] Handle a terminal result from a successful send before another move or close. The 409 path checks reply['result'], but the normal send path always appends the reply and continues. The kit's play() explicitly handles terminal results here (for example, the last supplier walking away). Otherwise we can call close() on an ended session, then call it again through the emergency path and lose an already available result. Save/return the terminal result immediately after committing the sent message. Add a fake-table regression asserting that close() is never called after send() returns a result.

=== 4238823506 buyer/policy.py:87 commit=4691536 reply_to=null
[P2] Do not interpret the first component's should-cost as the bundle's unit cost. For a multi-part case, full_cost feeds near_cost, the relationship target and the supplier estimate, but this lookup uses only parts[0]. A component cost and a kit price are different units. Derive a bundle estimate only from documented composition/quantities or an explicit bundle-level cost. If those are absent, keep the estimate unknown and disable estimate-dependent decisions rather than inventing equal weights. Add tests for a known composition and a bundle whose composition is unavailable.

e727ee8 Learnings: pushing past a final offer ends the case (D01)

# Agent design

The target architecture of our buyer, merged from the team's planning notes (PRs #7 to #10,
10 Oct). What we learned in play is in `learnings.md`; this file says what we build.

**Status.** The branch `steffen/price-engine` plays a code-only policy with a model-written
paragraph (`buyer/policy.py`, run by `buyer/runner.py`): practice mean of best scores 0.73 (from
0.32), sandbox D01 0.99, D02 0.73. What it does is under "Implemented" below; the rest of this file
is the target design. Julian's draft two (`origin/julian/draft-two`) holds a richer stance and
reader design that is not merged. The architecture diagram is on page 1 of
[how-it-works.pdf](how-it-works.pdf).

## Implemented (price engine)

| Module | Job |
|---|---|
| `buyer/economics.py` | C of a sheet; what a sheet is worth to the supplier (`supplier_value` plus overtime for a faster delivery than it quoted); term planning: every allowed combination priced at the supplier's own valuation, lowest C, ties to the supplier's side; the relationship-optimal price |

page 1 of [how-it-works.pdf](how-it-works.pdf).

## Principle

Code owns every number and every binding decision; the model reads replies and writes e-mails.
Score is total cost C, not price. Every step has a fallback that still sends a move within 60 s.

1	"""Plays cases with the policy. The arena answers one call per session at a time and each thread's
2	60-second clock runs from the supplier's reply, so one loop sends one message at a time, always to
3	the thread whose clock has run longest; finished threads get a short question before their clock
4	runs out while the others still negotiate; then the cheapest acceptable sheet is accepted.
5	`play_waves` is the kit's Live Final loop with this runner."""
6	
7	import functools
8	import json
9	import logging
10	import threading
11	import time
12	from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
13	from pathlib import Path
14	
15	from arena_kit.client import ArenaError
16	from arena_kit.play import ENDED, RemoteTable, fetch_documents, latest, moves_left, quota_used_up
17	
18	from .policy import Negotiator, Side, deadline_near, keepalive_message
19	
20	log = logging.getLogger("buyer")
21	RUNS = Path("logs/runs")
22	KEEPALIVE_AFTER_S = 35  # a finished thread gets a question this long after the supplier's reply
23	
24	
25	def play_case(table, case_id, pkg=None, deadline=None, complete=None):
26	    case, threads = table.open(case_id)
27	    if getattr(table, "done", None):  # resumed a case that had already ended
28	        return table.done
29	    for events in threads.values():
30	        for m in events:
31	            fetch_documents(table, m)
32	    neg = Negotiator(case, pkg, complete)
33	    for sid, events in threads.items():
34	        try:
35	            neg.setup(sid, events)
36	            if any(m.get("from") == "buyer" for m in events):  # resumed: continue the path
37	                neg.restore(sid, events)
38	        except Exception:  # one supplier's data must not lose the case
39	            log.exception("%s %s: setup failed", case_id, sid)
40	            neg.sides.setdefault(sid, Side(sid)).state = "done"
41	    failed = dict.fromkeys(threads, 0)
42	    replied = {sid: time.monotonic() for sid in threads}
43	    # round 1 goes out cheapest quote first: if a clock runs out, it is the least promising one's
44	    order = sorted(threads, key=lambda sid: neg.sides[sid].quote or float("inf"))
45	    rank = {sid: i for i, sid in enumerate(order)}
46	    result = None
47	
48	    def open_threads():
49	        return [s for s in threads if neg.sides[s].state not in ("done", "ended") and live(s)]
50	
51	    def live(sid):
52	        return latest(threads[sid]).get("status") not in ENDED
53	
54	    while not deadline_near(deadline):
55	        todo = sorted(open_threads(), key=lambda s: (replied[s], rank[s]))
56	        waiting = [
57	            s
58	            for s in threads
59	            if neg.sides[s].state == "done"
60	            and live(s)
61	            and todo
62	            and time.monotonic() - replied[s] > KEEPALIVE_AFTER_S
63	            and moves_left(case, threads[s]) > 0
64	        ]
65	        if not todo:
66	            break
67	        if waiting:  # a finished bidder whose clock runs out first: keep it alive
68	            sid = min(waiting, key=lambda s: replied[s])
69	            message = keepalive_message(threads[sid])
70	        else:
71	            sid = todo[0]
72	            try:
73	                move = neg.move(sid, threads)
74	            except Exception:  # a field the policy did not expect: the thread must not fall silent
75	                log.exception("%s %s: move failed", case_id, sid)
76	                failed[sid] += 1
77	                if failed[sid] > 2:
78	                    neg.sides[sid].state = "done"
79	                    continue
80	                move = neg.fallback_move(sid, threads)
81	            if move is None:
82	                continue
83	            message = move["message"]
84	        try:
85	            reply = table.send(sid, message)
86	        except ArenaError as e:
87	            if e.status != 409:
88	                raise
89	            log.info("%s %s: %s", case_id, sid, e.detail)
90	            neg.rollback(sid)  # it never got this message: our last offer stands for it
91	            reply = table.missed(sid, e)
92	            if "result" in reply:
93	                result = reply["result"]
94	                break
95	            threads[sid].append(reply)
96	            replied[sid] = time.monotonic()
97	            continue
98	        neg.commit(sid)
99	        threads[sid] += [{**message, "from": "buyer"}, reply]
100	        replied[sid] = time.monotonic()
101	    if result is None:
102	        for events in threads.values():  # the latest quote PDFs: standard terms for the close
103	            for m in events[-2:]:
104	                try:
105	                    fetch_documents(table, m)
106	                except ArenaError as e:
107	                    log.warning("%s: document not fetched: %s", case_id, e)
108	        try:
109	            decision = neg.close(threads)
110	            result = table.close(decision["supplier_id"], decision["message"])
111	        except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - a case must end with a decision
112	            log.warning("%s: close failed (%s), accepting a standing sheet", case_id, e)
113	            result = table.close(*neg.fallback_close(threads))
114	    save(table.session_id, case_id, neg, result)
115	    return result
116	
117	
118	def save(session_id, case_id, neg, result):
119	    RUNS.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
120	    keep = ("deal", "supplier_id", "terms", "c_open", "c_deal", "c_best", "score")
121	    path = RUNS / f"{case_id.split(':')[-1]}_{session_id}.json"
122	    out = {"case": case_id, "session": session_id, "notes": neg.notes, "result": {k: result.get(k) for k in keep}}
123	    path.write_text(json.dumps(out, indent=1, default=str))
124	
125	
126	def play_all(client, case_ids, pkg=None, parallel=8, complete=None):
127	    """Practice or sandbox: many cases at once. {case_id: result or the exception that stopped it}."""
128	    used_up = threading.Event()
129	
130	    def one(case_id):
131	        if used_up.is_set():
132	            return case_id, ArenaError(429, "not started: the practice quota is used up")
133	        try:
134	            return case_id, play_case(RemoteTable(client), case_id, pkg, complete=complete)
135	        except ArenaError as e:
136	            if quota_used_up(e):
137	                used_up.set()
138	            log.warning("%s: %s", case_id, e)
139	            return case_id, e
140	        except Exception as e:  # one broken case must not stop the others
141	            log.exception("%s failed", case_id)
142	            return case_id, e
143	
144	    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=parallel) as pool:
145	        return dict(pool.map(one, case_ids))
146	
147	
148	def play_waves(client, pkg=None, waves=5, parallel=10, poll=2.0, complete=None):
149	    """The Live Final: wait for each wave, play its cases in parallel within the wave's cap. No
150	    human may restart it, so nothing here raises: a failed poll is polled again, a crashed case is
151	    resumed once (the arena names the running session on a second open)."""
152	    started, closed, caps = {}, set(), {}
153	
154	    def one(case, deadline):
155	        for attempt in range(2):
156	            try:
157	                return play_case(RemoteTable(client, case), case["case_id"], pkg, deadline, complete)
158	            except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - one broken case must not stop the others
159	                log.exception("%s failed (attempt %d)", case["case_id"], attempt + 1)
160	                err = e
161	                time.sleep(2)
162	        return err
163	
164	    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=parallel) as pool:
165	        while len(closed) < waves or not all(f.done() for f in started.values()):
166	            try:
167	                cases = client.cases("final")
168	            except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - 403 before the first wave, a network blip: poll again
169	                if not (isinstance(e, ArenaError) and e.status == 403):
170	                    log.warning("case list: %s", e)
171	                cases = []
172	            for case in cases:
173	                if not case.get("open"):
174	                    closed.add(case["wave"])
175	                    continue
176	                if case.get("seconds_left") is not None:
177	                    caps[case["wave"]] = time.time() + case["seconds_left"]
178	                if case["case_id"] not in started and case.get("seconds_left"):
179	                    log.warning("wave %s: %s", case["wave"], case["case_id"])
180	                    started[case["case_id"]] = pool.submit(one, case, functools.partial(caps.get, case["wave"]))
181	            time.sleep(poll)
182	    return {case_id: f.result() for case_id, f in started.items()}
